newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says done enough to stop new peso attacks.
newsitem.headline: Manila says done enough to stop new peso attacks.

text.p: The Philippines has, for the moment, taken all the measures it needs to prevent another speculative attack on the peso, central bank governor Gabriel Singson said on Tuesday.
Earlier in the day, the central bank announced it had cut maximum long dollar positions of banks to five percent from 10 percent of their capital.
It also further raised liquidity reserves to four percent from three percent to siphon off excess money in the system that might be used for speculation.
"We will continue to look for loopholes. As of this time we feel that we have adopted all the measures that have to be taken. But tomorrow we might find something again," he told foreign reporters.

Since the July 11 effective peso devaulation, the central bank has adopted a series of measures to protect the peso, including preventing foreign banks operating in the Philippines from using the local spot currency market for their dollars.
Singson said he also thought the gap between the official and the parallel foreign exchange markets would narrow.
The rates, almost the same until July 11, have diverged though the difference has more recently narrowed again.
"Eventually these two markets will become the same, as before. These are temporary situations," he said.
He reiterated however that the central bank could not in the end go against market forces.

The reason for the attack on the peso was the result of a number of factors, he said, when asked if he agreed with some views that the recent plight of the southeast Asian currencies was the result of a conspiracy by speculators.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad last week named U.S. financier George Soros as the person behind the attacks. The U.S. government has dismissed the allegation.

Singson also urged local businessmen to wait a "little while" before interest rates can finally go back to normal, though they have already started to fall from the recent 2-1/2 year highs to protect the peso.
